1086.title: The dancer and the watcher
1086.hook: Samkhya's dancer: nature performs, the self watches, and yoga's 'just watch your thoughts' starts here
1086.carry: the mind is nature's dance; the self is the watcher
1086.tomorrow: The goddess says: I am Brahman
1086.howItsDone: The Samkhya Karika is studied in courses on Indian philosophy and in yoga schools, where its two principles, purusha and prakriti, are used to explain the Yoga Sutras.

segments.voice: Yesterday: even the mind is prakriti, God's nature. The Gita's list ran earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect and the sense of I, with a higher nature holding the world up.
screen: `ALL OF THIS IS MINE, AND THERE IS MORE.`

segments.voice: A dancer steps onto a stage. She moves, turns, tells a whole story with her hands and eyes. The audience watches. At some point the dance is complete: everything she came to show has been shown. So she stops, and walks off. That small scene is a picture from Samkhya, one of the philosophical schools of India, in a short book of verses called the Samkhya Karika. It's a cool, careful map of the world, not a hymn. But its picture of nature as a performer belongs right next to Shakti.
screen: `A DANCER, A STAGE, AN AUDIENCE.` → `EVERYTHING SHOWN, SHE STOPS.` → `A PICTURE FROM SAMKHYA.`

segments.voice: Samkhya names two principles. Purusha: pure awareness, the one who watches. Prakriti: nature, everything that moves and changes. Here's the surprise: in Samkhya, the mind sits on nature's side. Thoughts, moods, memory, even the sense of I: all of it is prakriti, part of the dance. The self is the one watching. The verse, in paraphrase: as a dancer stops after showing herself to the audience, so prakriti stops after showing herself to purusha. Why does she dance at all? The Samkhya Karika says nature works for the watcher's sake, so it can see, and be free. And the tenderest line: nothing is more modest than prakriti. Once she knows she's been seen, she does not show herself again. So here is the teaching: you are not the storm of thoughts; you are the one who sees it. Many teachers read Samkhya's freedom just this way: the watcher no longer mistaking the dance for itself. The Yoga Sutras build on this map. Yoga, they say, is the stilling of the mind's turnings, and then the seer rests in its own nature. So when a yoga class says just watch your thoughts, that isn't a wellness slogan. It's a Hindu map of the self. Today: the night before something big, the mind stages every way it could go wrong. Samkhya doesn't tell you to fight the show. It tells you who's in the audience. One difference to keep: in Samkhya, prakriti isn't a goddess. Goddess traditions take the same picture and say the dancer is Shakti herself. That's tomorrow.
screen: `PURUSHA WATCHES. PRAKRITI MOVES.` · `NOTHING MORE MODEST THAN PRAKRITI.` · `YOU ARE NOT THE STORM OF THOUGHTS.` · `THEN THE SEER RESTS IN ITSELF.` · then, large: `YOU ARE THE ONE WATCHING.`

segments.voice: Sit still and let yourself be the audience: thoughts, sounds and feelings will come onstage, a plan, a passing car, an itch. Don't chase any of them off; watch each one the way you'd watch a dancer, with interest, until it has finished showing itself and leaves. If you pray, you can rest in the name you use for the divine; if you don't, rest in the watching.
Shakti as a philosophy. In Samkhya, prakriti dances for purusha, the watcher, and when she has been fully seen, she stops.
Your line: the mind is nature's dance; the self is the watcher. Until tomorrow.

1087.title: The goddess says: I am Brahman
1087.hook: all the gods ask the goddess who she is, and her answer is why so many Hindus call God Ma
1087.carry: the goddess is Brahman itself, not a sidekick
1087.howItsDone: The Devi Upanishad, also called the Devi Atharvashirsha, is chanted by worshippers of the goddess, including during Navaratri, and is studied as a statement of the goddess as ultimate reality.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the mind is nature's dance; the self is the watcher. Samkhya's dancer shows herself, and once she's been fully seen, she stops.

Who are you? It's the question you ask a stranger at the door, a new neighbor, a voice on the phone. In a short text called the Devi Upanishad, it's the question every god asks the goddess. They come and stand before her, all of them together, and ask: who are you, great goddess? Yesterday, in Samkhya, nature danced and said nothing. Today she is asked to speak for herself. And her answer isn't a name, or a family, or a list of victories.
screen: `ALL THE GODS COME TO HER.` → `WHO ARE YOU, GREAT GODDESS?` → `TODAY SHE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Here's her answer, in paraphrase. I am of the very nature of Brahman. From me comes this world, made of prakriti and purusha, nature and spirit. I am joy and not-joy. I am knowing and not-knowing. First, she answers with Brahman, the one ultimate reality the Upanishads point to. Not a goddess beside God. The goddess says: that's me. Second, the pair. Yesterday Samkhya kept prakriti and purusha apart, the dancer and the watcher. Here both come from her. She is the dance and the one watching it. Third, the opposites. Joy and not-joy, knowing and not-knowing. She doesn't keep only the comfortable half. In Shakta eyes, that's why the same Devi can be gentle Lakshmi on a lotus and fierce Kali with a sword: one power, many faces. Fourth, the gods bow and praise her. This is the heart of Shakta Hinduism, one of the tradition's great streams: the highest reality is worshipped as the Goddess, the Mother. It's why so many Hindus simply call God Ma, why pilgrims climbing to the shrine of Vaishno Devi call out Jai Mata Di, victory to the Mother, and why Navaratri gives nine nights to her. Not everyone on the Hindu path puts it this way. Vaishnava and Shaiva traditions name the highest reality Vishnu or Shiva. But in this Upanishad, the goddess answers for herself. Today: when someone hears goddess and pictures a sidekick, this text is the answer. Ask her who she is, and she doesn't give a husband's name. She says: everything.
screen: `I AM OF THE NATURE OF BRAHMAN.` · `PRAKRITI AND PURUSHA, BOTH FROM HER.` · `ONE POWER, MANY FACES.` · `GOD AS MA.` · then, large: `WHO ARE YOU? I AM BRAHMAN.`

segments.voice: Notice one comfortable thing right now, warmth or a soft seat, and hold it for a few breaths. Then notice one uncomfortable thing, a tight shoulder or a worry, and hold that too, without pushing it away, letting both sit in the same space the way the goddess holds joy and not-joy. If you pray, you can rest in the name of the Devi, or the name you use for God; if you don't, rest in the space that holds both.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Devi Upanishad, the gods ask who she is, and she answers: of the nature of Brahman, the source of prakriti and purusha both.
Your line: the goddess is Brahman itself, not a sidekick. Asked who she is, she answers with everything. I'll be here tomorrow.

1088.title: Half Shiva, half Parvati
1088.hook: a poet bows to a couple joined like a word and its meaning, and a sage learns he can't honor one without the other
1088.carry: Shiva and Shakti: two, and never apart
1088.howItsDone: The opening verse of Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha is learned by students of Sanskrit and recited as an invocation, and images of Ardhanarishvara, half Shiva and half Parvati, stand in temples dedicated to Shiva.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the goddess is Brahman itself, not a sidekick. The gods asked who are you, and she answered, of the nature of Brahman.

A poet sits down to write a long poem about the kings of Raghu's line, one king after another. And the first thing he writes isn't about any king. It's about a word and its meaning. The poet is Kalidasa, whose Parvati this path met in the forest not long ago. Before he tells a single story, he bows to a couple. Not a king and queen: Shiva and Parvati. And he chooses one picture to say how close they are.
screen: `A LONG POEM OF KINGS.` → `FIRST: A WORD AND ITS MEANING.` → `HE BOWS TO A COUPLE.`

segments.voice: Here is the verse, in paraphrase. Joined like word and meaning, for the sake of understanding word and meaning, I bow to the parents of the world, Parvati and Shiva. A word without meaning is just noise; a meaning needs a word to carry it. Two, and never apart. That's how close the poet says the god and the goddess are. A temple story makes the same point with a body. A sage named Bhringi loved Shiva so single-mindedly that he would circle only Shiva in worship, never Parvati. So, as the story is told, Parvati drew close and became one body with Shiva, half and half. In some tellings Bhringi still tried to squeeze between them. The story's point is plain: you cannot honor one without the other. That shared body is Ardhanarishvara, the lord who is half woman: on one side Shiva, ash and matted hair; on the other Parvati, earring and silk. It's carved in temples to this day. Here's the teaching. In Hindu thought, Shiva and Shakti aren't two gods who happen to be married. Many teachers read them as awareness and power, the still and the moving, neither complete alone. Remember the hymn this path met earlier: without Shakti, Shiva cannot even stir. Today: a Hindu wife is often called ardhangini, the half of the body. Some people hear that and think it makes her half a person. Ardhanarishvara says the opposite. Even God, in this picture, is only whole as two.
screen: `JOINED LIKE WORD AND MEANING.` · `BHRINGI CIRCLES ONLY SHIVA.` · `ONE BODY: HALF SHIVA, HALF PARVATI.` · `STILL AND MOVING, NEITHER ALONE.` · then, large: `TWO, AND NEVER APART.`

segments.voice: Choose one simple word that matters to you, home, mother, peace, a name, and say it once, silently, then watch what arrives with it: a picture, a feeling, a face. Say it again, slowly, and rest wherever the sound and the sense meet. If you pray, you can choose the name of the goddess, or Shiva, or the name you use for God.
Shakti as a philosophy. Kalidasa bows to Parvati and Shiva, the parents of the world, joined like a word and its meaning.
Your line: Shiva and Shakti, two, and never apart. See you tomorrow.

1089.title: Vak, the goddess who speaks
1089.hook: a Rig Veda hymn where the goddess of speech says I, and why Hindus treat sacred sound with care
1089.carry: Vak: the goddess is the power in every word
1089.howItsDone: This hymn, Rig Veda 10.125, is known as the Devi Sukta or Vak Sukta; it is chanted in goddess worship, and some recite it alongside the Devi Mahatmya.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shiva and Shakti, two, and never apart. A word and its meaning, and one body, half and half.

I. A hymn can be sung to Agni, to Indra, to the dawn. This one in the Rig Veda is sung by someone. The speaker is Vak, a goddess whose name means speech, and tradition names the hymn's seer as Vak, daughter of the sage Ambhrina: a woman's voice among the Rig Veda's seers. The whole hymn comes from her own mouth. I move with the gods. I hold them up. I bend the bow. I breathe out like the wind.
screen: `NOT SUNG TO HER. SUNG BY HER.` → `VAK: THE GODDESS WHO IS SPEECH.` → `SHE SPEAKS AS I.`

segments.voice: Here is some of the hymn, in paraphrase. I move with the Rudras and the Vasus, with the Adityas and all the gods. I hold up Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni. I am the queen, the gatherer of treasures. Through me eats the one who eats, the one who sees, breathes and hears. Without knowing it, they live in me. I bend the bow for Rudra. I breathe out like the wind, taking hold of all the worlds. So great have I become. First, she holds the gods up, not the other way around. Second, she's inside ordinary acts: eating, seeing, breathing, hearing, all done through her, without knowing it. Third, she reaches beyond the sky and the earth. Inside everything, and beyond it. Here is the teaching. In Hindu thought, speech isn't only noise we make. Vak is divine power, Shakti, as sound. That's why a mantra is learned carefully, syllable by syllable, why chanting begins with Om, and why later tradition honors speech and learning as the goddess Saraswati. Many who recite the Devi Mahatmya add this very hymn, the Devi Sukta. Today: we spend words all day, in texts, comments, the thing said too fast. In this hymn, speech is not a tool we own; it is her. Some teachers draw a plain lesson from it: treat your words as hers, on loan, and spend them with care. Tomorrow the path turns to a hymn sung to a goddess: the Sri Sukta.
screen: `I MOVE WITH THE GODS. I HOLD THEM UP.` · `THROUGH ME, THEY EAT, SEE, BREATHE.` · `VAK: SHAKTI AS SOUND.` · `WHY A MANTRA IS SAID WITH CARE.` · then, large: `THE POWER IN EVERY WORD.`

segments.voice: Let the breath come on its own, and notice it as the hymn does: something breathing through you, not only something you do. Then add hearing, the sounds arriving without effort, and seeing, light on the eyelids or the room, and rest in all of it at once. If you pray, you can hold the word Devi, or Ma, with the out-breath; if you don't, just rest in the breathing.
Shakti as a philosophy. In the Rig Veda, Vak speaks for herself: through her the world eats, sees, breathes and hears, and she breathes out like the wind.
Your line: Vak, the goddess is the power in every word. Go gently.

1090.title: Lakshmi rises from the ocean
1090.hook: the gods churn the ocean, the moon rises, then Lakshmi on a lotus: the goddess the Sri Sukta paints in gold and moonlight
1090.carry: Lakshmi is Shakti as abundance, not only money
1090.howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted in Lakshmi worship, including in some homes and temples at Diwali, with lamps lit and offerings set before an image of the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vak, the goddess is the power in every word. I move with the gods; I breathe out like the wind.

Picture an ocean churned like milk into butter. The gods pull one end of a great serpent, the asuras pull the other, and a mountain spins in the sea between them. In the Vishnu Purana's telling, wonders rise from the foam, one after another. The moon rises. More wonders follow. And then, standing on a lotus, shining, comes Sri, the goddess Lakshmi. Elephants pour water over her from golden jars, and she goes to Vishnu. Today, the hymn Hindus still chant when lamps are lit for her: the Sri Sukta.
screen: `THE OCEAN, CHURNED.` → `THE MOON RISES. THEN SRI, ON A LOTUS.` → `THE HYMN TO SRI.`

segments.voice: Sukta means hymn, and sri is heard as radiance, beauty and good fortune all at once. The hymn's first verse paints her, in paraphrase: golden in color, wearing garlands of gold and silver, shining like the moon, made of gold. Notice the pair. Gold you can earn, store and spend. Moonlight nobody can own. And in the churning story, the moon and Lakshmi rise from the same sea. Some readers hear the hymn's point there: the fortune it asks for is bright like gold and freely given like moonlight. Here's the teaching. Lakshmi is Shakti, the goddess's power, seen as abundance. Not only money: food on the table, health, a peaceful house, a good name. That's why Lakshmi Puja on Diwali night isn't a bank meeting. Families clean the house, draw rangoli at the door, light lamps and leave the way open, because abundance is a goddess you welcome, not a thing you grab. Business families set their new account books before her too: work honored, not money worshipped for its own sake. Teachers read the hymn more than one way. Some keep it plain, a household asking not to go without. Others hear it inwardly, as a prayer for the brightness of a good life. The hymn doesn't choose. Today: we measure a good month in one number. The Sri Sukta's portrait counts in gold and moonlight both.
screen: `SUKTA: A HYMN. SRI: RADIANCE, FORTUNE.` · `GOLDEN, GARLANDED, MOONLIT.` · `THE MOON AND LAKSHMI, FROM ONE SEA.` · `SHAKTI, SEEN AS ABUNDANCE.` · then, large: `WELCOMED, NOT GRABBED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that's like gold, something you worked for or keep safe, and hold it for a few breaths, with thanks. Then bring to mind one thing like moonlight, something good you never earned and can't own: a friend's laugh, a clear night, a stranger's kindness. If you pray, you can name them both before Lakshmi, or before God, in the words you already use.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn to Sri, called Lakshmi, which opens by seeing her golden, garlanded in gold and silver, and shining like the moon.
Your line: Lakshmi is Shakti as abundance, not only money. Gold you can keep; moonlight you can only see. That's today, done.

1091.title: Agni, the go-between
1091.hook: the fire god once hid from his job, and the gods coaxed him back: why every puja still has a flame
1091.carry: Agni carries the offering; the lamp invites her
1091.howItsDone: In Lakshmi worship and Vedic rites, the Sri Sukta is chanted before a lamp or sacred fire, and some households light small lamps at Diwali to welcome the goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Lakshmi is Shakti as abundance, not only money. She rose from the churned ocean, and the Sri Sukta paints her golden and moonlit.

Even a god can want to quit. In one Rig Veda hymn, Agni, the fire, has had enough. His work is to carry the offerings to the gods, and he's afraid of it: the brothers who held that work before him are gone. So he hides, in the waters and in the plants. The gods go looking, find him, and coax him back, promising him a share of the offerings. He agrees. In the Vedic picture, fire has carried things between earth and heaven ever since. Which is why the Sri Sukta's first request isn't to the goddess at all. It's to the fire.
screen: `AGNI HIDES FROM HIS WORK.` → `THE GODS COAX HIM BACK.` → `BRING HER TO ME, FIRE.`

segments.voice: The verse ends, in paraphrase: O Jatavedas, bring Lakshmi to me. Jatavedas is a name of Agni. In the Rig Veda's very first hymn, Agni is praised as the priest of the sacrifice, the one who will bring the gods here. Offerings go into the fire; the fire brings the gods. The word for bring is avaha: bring here, carry this way. Not go and get. More like a host saying, please bring her by. Here's the teaching. In Hindu worship, fire is the go-between. It's why a havan pours ghee and grain into a flame: the fire carries the offering. It's why a Hindu wedding is walked around a fire, with Agni as witness. It's why so many pujas end with aarti: a lamp waved before the deity, then families cup their hands over the flame and draw its warmth to their eyes and heads. And it's why, at Diwali, small lamps line windowsills and doorsteps. In the Sri Sukta's picture, a light kept burning is how the goddess is asked to come. The verse quietly assumes one more thing: you can't ask a fire for anything if none is burning. Someone has to keep it fed. Some readers hear a plain lesson there: fortune is asked for through something you already keep alive at home. Today: string lights are pretty. But a clay lamp with a wick in oil is an invitation, and lighting it is a prayer.
screen: `JATAVEDAS: A NAME OF AGNI, THE FIRE.` · `FIRE IS THE GO-BETWEEN.` · `HAVAN, WEDDING FIRE, AARTI.` · `A LAMP AT THE DOOR FOR LAKSHMI.` · then, large: `THE LAMP INVITES HER.`

segments.voice: Picture a small household fire, low and steady: with each in-breath, lay one small stick on it; with each out-breath, watch it settle and glow, not too much, not too little. If you pray, you can ask the fire, as the hymn does, to bring good fortune to your house, or speak to God in your own words; if you don't, let the flame stand for whatever you hope will come.
The Sri Sukta. In its opening verse, the singer asks Jatavedas, the fire, to bring Lakshmi: the fire as the go-between.

1092.title: The Lakshmi who stays
1092.hook: Indra lets a sage's garland be trampled and fortune leaves the worlds; the Sri Sukta asks for the Lakshmi who does not go away
1092.carry: Lakshmi stays where she is honored
1092.howItsDone: The Sri Sukta is chanted by some Hindus in Lakshmi worship at home and in temples, including at Diwali, and some families recite it on Fridays.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Agni carries the offering; the lamp invites her. Fire is the go-between. Today, why the gods needed her back at all.

A sage hands the king of the gods a garland. Indra, riding his great white elephant, drops it onto the elephant's head, and the elephant flings it to the ground and tramples it. In the Vishnu Purana, the sage, Durvasa, is furious: because you scorned this, he says, your fortune will leave you. And it does. Sri walks out of the three worlds. Plants wither. Nothing shines. That's why the gods had to churn the ocean, the story this week began with: to bring her back.
screen: `A GARLAND, TRAMPLED.` → `SRI LEAVES THE THREE WORLDS.` → `CHURN THE OCEAN, BRING HER BACK.`

segments.voice: When Lakshmi rose again, the Vishnu Purana says, Indra praised her with a hymn and asked for one thing: never leave the three worlds again. She agreed. The Sri Sukta asks the same, in its own words. In paraphrase: bring me, Jatavedas, that Lakshmi who does not go away, in whom I may find gold, cattle, horses and people. One long word: anapagamini, the one who does not go away. You only ask for someone who stays if you know what it is when someone leaves. Tradition calls Lakshmi restless. Here's the teaching, as many Hindus understand it: Lakshmi stays where she is honored. Indra lost her not by being poor but by treating a gift as nothing. That's why so many Hindu homes treat fortune like a guest. If a foot touches money or a book, a child is taught to touch it and bring the hand to the forehead, a small sorry. A first paycheck is often set before the family shrine, or offered to elders, before a rupee or a dollar is spent. And look at the hymn's list: gold, cattle, horses, and last, people. The faces around the table are counted among the riches. Today: a paycheck lands Friday and is gone by Thursday. The Sri Sukta doesn't promise more of it. It asks for the fortune with roots, and the story says how she's kept: with respect, not grabbing. A week behind us: the watcher, the goddess who is Brahman, two who are never apart, the voice in every word, and Lakshmi, rising, invited by fire, asked to stay.
screen: `INDRA ASKS: NEVER LEAVE AGAIN.` · `THE ONE WHO DOES NOT GO AWAY.` · `SHE STAYS WHERE SHE IS HONORED.` · `GOLD, CATTLE, HORSES, PEOPLE.` · then, large: `COME, AND DON'T GO.`

segments.voice: Notice the breath first: it leaves, and it comes back, without being asked. Then bring to mind one good thing in your life that hasn't gone away, a friend who keeps answering, a kitchen, a song that's still there, and rest with it, letting the thanks be quiet. If you pray, you can name it before Lakshmi or before God, in the words you already use; if you don't, let the steady thing be enough.
